title: The Sevapanthis
hookLine: followers of Bhai Kanhaiya, devoted to quiet service

lines: A FEW STAY TO STACK THE CHAIRS.
cards: At the end of a big event, the speakers get the applause and the photos. Then the hall empties, and a few people stay behind. They stack the chairs, wipe the tables, carry the bins out to the curb in the dark.
Nobody films that part. In year one you met Bhai Kanhaiya, the water carrier on the battlefield who, the story says, saw his Guru's face in every wounded man. That was one day of his life.
Today is about what came after him: people who made the stay-behind part their whole way of life.

teach.b: The word is Sevapanthi: one who walks the path of seva, selfless service. Tradition says Bhai Kanhaiya's companions and followers formed a community around his way, and that community still exists.
Tradition remembers three things about them. First, service is the center, not a side activity.

teach.h: REST, WATER AND FOOD FOR ANYONE.
teach.b: Sevapanthis are remembered for running places where travelers could rest, drink and eat, and for tending the sick, without asking who anyone was. Second, they lived by their own work.

teach.h: BREAD EARNED BY THEIR OWN HANDS.
teach.b: Tradition says they didn't go begging for alms and earned their bread with their hands; serving others while asking nothing of them was the point.
Third, quietness: they're remembered less for great deeds with names attached than for steady work over a long time.

teach.h: SRI RAAG: SERVE HERE, A SEAT THERE.
teach.b: In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak gives a short line on seva. In paraphrase: do seva in this world, and you will find a place to sit in the Lord's court.
Notice where the service happens: in this world, among people, in kitchens and on roads. And notice the reward: not applause, a seat, the way a tired traveler finds one at a Sevapanthi rest stop.

Some Sikhs hear echoes of this in the langar, and in the shoe room at the gurdwara, where volunteers polish strangers' shoes. The Sevapanthis took that common Sikh practice and made it the name of their path.
Not service as a break from real life; service as the real life, with the rest fitted in around it.

how: Sevapanthis, who trace their community to Bhai Kanhaiya, are remembered for serving travelers and the sick and for living by their own work; seva in the langar and the shoe room is part of everyday Sikh life.

o: a pilgrim who walks to every Sikh shrine
a soldier who carries water into battle
one who walks the path of selfless service

games.q: inside the Sevapanthis: tap the pairs.
p: one on the path of seva
the community traces itself to him
serve here, find a seat in the court

s: tradition says the Sevapanthis lived by begging
tradition says they didn't go begging; they earned their bread by their own work.
tradition says Bhai Kanhaiya's followers formed it, and it continues.
Guru Nanak places seva somewhere far from ordinary life
in Sri Raag: do seva in this world, and find a seat in the Lord's court.

games.q: you run a free water stall on a hot road, the Sevapanthi way. a grateful traveler tries to press money into your hand. what does tradition say they did?
o: take it; the stall has costs.
decline, and keep serving from what your own work earns.
games.why: tradition says Sevapanthis didn't seek alms; they earned their bread with their own hands and served anyone for free.

practice: Think of one small job in the hours ahead that nobody will thank you for, a dish in the sink, a shared space to tidy, and picture yourself doing it quietly and walking away without mentioning it.
Breathe out the wish to be seen, and if you pray, rest on Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Sevapanthi. One on the path of seva: a community that, tradition says, follows Bhai Kanhaiya, living by its own work and serving anyone. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: selfless service. a Sevapanthi is one on its path.

carryVoice: Your line: service first. The seat comes without the applause, and that is enough. Until tomorrow.
